reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it provides procedural education about YouTube monetization, including eligibility thresholds, payment steps, memberships, and advertising revenue. It separately promotes a training course about making money through YouTube, while the requests to subscribe and follow social accounts are ordinary audience engagement. The described material does not establish a deceptive payment, credential, investment, or victim-loss mechanism.

citations.quote: How To Get Paid On YouTube (NEW Easy Steps)
you need to have got 1,000 subscribers or more on your channel
you need to have totalled up 4,000 hours of watch time
The most commonly known way that you're going to get paid through your channel. Is for the ads that YouTube shows on your videos.
you can set up memberships on your channel and get paid a monthly subscription from anyone. That signs up as a member.

opening.argument: The video links the prospect of earning money to a sequence of viewer commitments: building a qualifying channel, enabling monetization, and then pursuing additional income routes. It also directs viewers toward a paid course promising instruction on making “as much money as possible” through YouTube. That combination makes the offer functionally solicitation-oriented, even though the requested action is channel activity or course purchase rather than a conventional deposit. The title presents getting paid as involving “NEW Easy Steps,” while the spoken guidance adds substantial eligibility requirements and an approval process. A careful judge can therefore view the reward-action framing as insufficiently qualified: viewers are steered toward actions and a commercial training product by an income-oriented promise.

citations.quote: How To Get Paid On YouTube (NEW Easy Steps)
you need to have got 1,000 subscribers or more on your channel
It's an eight hour long course focusing on making as much money as possible through your. YouTube channel
you'll get step-by-step. Instructions through that training

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls this procedural education, but the central framing is still an income solicitation: the title promises easy steps to get paid, the video enumerates multiple monetization routes, and it ends by directing viewers toward paid training. Explaining thresholds does not resolve whether the commercial pitch overstates accessibility or likely outcomes. The evidence supports a connected chain of income expectations, channel participation, and course purchase, not merely neutral platform documentation.

citations.quote: How To Get Paid On YouTube (NEW Easy Steps)
Here's the three easiest ways you can make even more money through your YouTube channel.
You can get it by clicking the link below

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material does not promise that viewers will receive money simply for clicking, registering, or buying the course. It describes YouTube eligibility and several possible revenue features, including requirements of 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 hours of watch time. The course invitation is disclosed as a product promotion, and neither the title nor the sales language establishes guaranteed earnings, a payment to the promoter as a condition of withdrawing funds, or victim loss.

citations.quote: you need to have got 1,000 subscribers or more on your channel
you need to have totalled up 4,000 hours of watch time
It's an eight hour long course focusing on making as much money as possible through your. YouTube channel

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: the headline emphasizes “NEW Easy Steps,” the description repeatedly focuses on getting paid and monthly payments, and the speaker advertises a course as “Dirt Cheap” while promising instruction on making as much money as possible. The video also supplies multiple external destinations, including a course link and further money-making videos. None of that proves a fraudulent outcome by itself, but the combination creates a promotional funnel around an attractive income theme. The presentation foregrounds monetization while the practical barriers, approval uncertainty, and dependence on audience performance make the promised accessibility materially less clear.

citations.quote: How To Get Paid On YouTube (NEW Easy Steps)
They show you exactly what is required to go through to join the YouTube Partner Program and to receive monthly payments
In between each payment that YouTube sends you,. You're going to have to have made $100 on your channel
it's Dirt Cheap

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the links ordinary resources overlooks that the description places a paid course beside claims about obtaining monthly YouTube payments, while the video advertises several additional ways to make money. The “Dirt Cheap” pitch and “as much money as possible” framing amplify the appeal beyond a dry technical explanation. The fact that some requirements are mentioned does not eliminate the risk that the overall presentation attracts viewers with easy-income language and then routes them to external commercial material.

citations.quote: MAKING MONEY ON YOUTUBE (COURSE)
Shameless plug you can. Learn about all the options I've learned of that are available to YouTubers
It's an eight hour long course focusing on making as much money as possible

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary promotional and informational signals, not evidence of a scam mechanism. The description identifies the course as a course and gives links to YouTube-related resources; it does not promise guaranteed or unusually easy returns. The video expressly states that monetization requires substantial audience and watch-time thresholds, and approval can take time. Those qualifications undercut the claim that the material conceals its practical barriers or presents effortless income.

citations.quote: YouTube will actually send you an email notification once your channel has passed. 4,000 hours of watch time and 1,000 subscribers
you'll have to wait a maximum of 30 days
The YouTube payment system has changed

opening.argument: Although the speaker adopts the role of an educator, the structure visibly shifts into promotion. The video announces “different ways to make money,” includes a visual “SALES TIME” cue, and then delivers a personal sales pitch for an eight-hour course with a link below. The speaker also describes the course as covering the best way to use every available monetization option. That makes the operational explanation a vehicle for steering viewers toward a commercial product and continued engagement, rather than purely independent guidance. The educational wrapper therefore does not resolve the income-acquisition concern; it may be precisely what makes the promotion more persuasive.

citations.quote: Shameless plug you can. Learn about all the options I've learned of that are available to YouTubers
You can get it by clicking the link below

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense separates the course promotion from the educational material, but the video itself places them in one continuous sales-oriented presentation. The monetization tutorial establishes the audience's desire to earn, then the speaker presents his own training as the way to learn all available options. The on-screen “SALES TIME” cue makes the promotional turn explicit. Ordinary subscription requests do not explain why the commercial pitch is embedded in advice about obtaining income.

citations.quote: It's an eight hour long course focusing on making as much money as possible through your. YouTube channel
through my own digital. Products

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion does not equal fraud. The speaker openly labels the course as his own digital product and calls the mention a “Shameless plug,” so viewers are not being tricked about the commercial relationship. The surrounding content remains a tutorial about platform requirements and monetization features. The cited sales cue and course link show advertising, but they fail to show a false payment promise, concealed fee, deceptive credential request, or loss mechanism.
